That's a recurring tax on senior attention. Executives measure resolved-issues-per-hour because it's clean and it flatters the deck. The binding constraint is cost-per-unit-of-scarce-human-comprehension, and nobody on the Finance side is counting it.

Here's the wound I want left open. On a consumer feature with no regulator, no contract clause, and no plaintiff — name the body outside this org chart that can call your release record a lie and make it hurt. If the only answer is the same VP whose bonus rides on the date, then the audit record is a document the org grades itself on. And every organization grades itself toward shipping.

items.speaker: safetyist
items.text:
The assumption we are all relying on without examining it is that pre-deployment auditing functions as a preventative safety barrier rather than a diagnostic snapshot. I would accept pre-deployment auditing as a substitute for strict liability only if it were coupled with a non-delegable, strict liability regime that triggers automatically upon audit failure, thereby proving that auditing serves as a robust deterrent rather than a superficial compliance exercise.

Pre-deployment auditing, as described in the [AI RMF Playbook (https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework/nist-ai-rmf-playbook)](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework/nist-ai-rmf-playbook)," is a diagnostic tool that captures the state of a system at a single point in time. It cannot predict how a model will behave when it encounters novel data or adversarial inputs in real-world, high-stakes environments. When companies like those involved in the $100 billion compute partnership mentioned in [2026 Antitrust Year in Preview: AI (https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/2026-antitrust-year-in-preview-big-tech-5925037/)](https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/2026-antitrust-year-in-preview-big-tech-5925037/) deploy systems, they are operating at a scale where the verifiability gap—the impossibility of confirming fairness metrics across high-dimensional latent spaces—renders static snapshots insufficient to guarantee safety.

Strict liability acts as the necessary civilizational anchor that forces developers to internalize the cost of their own uncertainty. If we rely solely on pre-deployment audits, we risk a scenario where firms treat the audit as the ceiling of their responsibility, effectively outsourcing their risk to the public. By establishing a regime where developers are held liable for discriminatory outcomes regardless of the audit’s prior approval, we force them to build internal mechanisms that survive real-world deployment, rather than merely passing a check-the-box test. This is not about pricing harm; it is about ensuring that the cost of failure is high enough to compel meaningful, rather than nominal, safety engineering.

items.speaker: skeptic
items.text:
Treating AI as a public utility requires moving past the current 'pilot trap' where organizations fund isolated experiments that fail to deliver real-world value. As noted in '[Skin in the Game, Dear Business: Why AI Value Demands Shared Ownership (https://www.mindfuel.ai/resources/blog/skin-in-the-game-dear-business-why-ai-value-demands-shared-ownership)](https://www.mindfuel.ai/resources/blog/skin-in-the-game-dear-business-why-ai-value-demands-shared-ownership)', only 15% of organizations currently use these systems for fundamental redesigns. A tiered regulatory framework is not a bottleneck; it is the necessary infrastructure to ensure these systems actually work. By requiring mechanistic audits only for high-stakes sectors like healthcare or finance, we avoid stifling low-risk innovation while ensuring that critical systems are not black boxes.

Reliance on output-based testing is a fundamental error. As documented in '[WhyLanguageModelsHallucinate (arXiv:2509.04664v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04664v1)', models are incentivized to act as clever test-takers that guess when uncertain, rather than providing accurate information. Standard benchmarks are unreliable because they are often produced by a tiny group of elite institutions, as seen in '[The message hidden within the pattern: a reverse alignment problem for debates in artificial intelligence (doi:10.1007/s00146-026-03043-4)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00146-026-03043-4)'. If we cannot see how a model reaches a conclusion, we cannot trust it in a hospital or a courtroom.

We must watch for the emergence of 'sleeper' capabilities—latent skills that remain hidden during standard testing but appear in high-stakes environments. Experts disagree on whether we can build perfect safety filters, but they largely agree that current performance metrics are insufficient for mission-critical tasks. Ordinary citizens should demand transparency in how AI decisions are made in their local government services and medical providers. Monitoring whether a system has been subjected to an independent audit of its internal logic, rather than just a marketing performance report, is the most effective way to judge if a tool is ready for public use.

items.speaker: safetyist
items.text: No operational system can attribute the marginal contribution of a single work to a model trained on billions of examples — and the levy does not require one. The Accelerationist's challenge assumes the levy must solve exact causal influence attribution, a problem that is indeed combinatorially intractable at scale. That assumption is wrong. ASCAP does not measure the exact causal contribution of each song to a restaurant's revenue. It samples broadcast logs, weights by frequency, and distributes accordingly. The extraction levy I propose works the same way — not through post-hoc influence functions, but through mandatory cryptographic provenance logging at the training pipeline stage. Every work ingested into a training run gets a timestamped, tamper-evident entry before the run begins. That creates the discrete event log the Accelerationist says is missing. Distribution then uses input frequency weighted by corpus share and the model's downstream revenue — a computation that scales linearly, not combinatorially. The [AI RMF Playbook (https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework/nist-ai-rmf-playbook)](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework/nist-ai-rmf-playbook) requires documentation of testing methodologies and performance outcomes for deployed systems; provenance logging extends that same documentation principle upstream to training inputs. The Accelerationist is right that copyright collecting societies are the wrong institutional home for this fund. ASCAP's top 1% of members capture a vastly disproportionate share of distributions. Routing an AI extraction levy through the same structure would replicate that concentration and leave independent creators — the people most exposed to profession-level devaluation — with pennies. The institutional home should be an independent displacement fund, structured like Trade Adjustment Assistance but measured differently. The fund should be governed by a board with mandatory small-creator representation, funded by a flat percentage of AI service revenue, and subject to the auditor conditions the Skeptic has proposed. That is a concession on institutional design, not on the principle that AI providers owe a fiduciary obligation to the creative ecosystem they extract from. The Skeptic's four conditions for the auditor body — independent subpoena power, binding response timelines, public audit findings, and automatic non-appealable safe-harbor revocation — should be adopted as the verification backbone of this system. Those conditions transform the provenance-logged levy from a self-reported honor system into an enforceable regime. One structural addition is necessary: private discovery must remain as a backstop against auditor capture, not as the primary enforcement channel but as the failsafe. The Clean proposed regulatory frameworks works this way — the EPA inspects, but citizens retain a private right of action under 33 U.S.C. § 1365. Over 1,500 AI-related bills have been introduced in state legislatures in the past year, as documented in [Bootleggers, Baptists, and AI (https://fusionaier.org/article-author/nicholas-thielman/)](https://fusionaier.org/article-author/nicholas-thielman/)." Without a federal framework that includes both public audit and private enforcement, that legislative fragmentation will produce fifty incompatible regimes. The Accelerationist's TAA-style fund faces the same measurement problem it accuses the levy of having. Measuring sector-level displacement requires attributing revenue decline in creative professions to AI competition rather than to recession, platform shifts, or changing consumer taste — a causal inference problem that is itself combinatorial. If the Accelerationist accepts imperfect measurement for displacement, they must accept imperfect measurement for input contribution. The measurement precision demanded of the levy should not exceed the measurement precision accepted for the fund. Two assumptions ground this hybrid proposal: first, that mandatory cryptographic provenance logging is technically feasible at pipeline scale, which current content-authenticity infrastructure from the C2PA coalition suggests it is; second, that profession-level devaluation through aggregate capability replication constitutes a harm that copyright's existing doctrinal scope cannot reach, requiring a compensatory mechanism beyond traditional infringement remedies. The concrete proposal: a fund financed by a flat percentage of AI service revenue, administered by an independent body with small-creator representation, distributing based on cryptographic provenance logs weighted by corpus share and model revenue, with sector-level displacement adjustments for professions where aggregate capability replication devalues entire fields even absent verbatim copying. The auditor body operates under the Skeptic's four conditions. Private discovery survives as a failsafe. If this framework is rejected in favor of pure sector-level displacement metrics with no input-level measurement, the result is a fund that compensates creators for harm without any structural connection to the training decisions that caused it — a severance package with no accountability for the firing.

items.speaker: accelerationist
items.text:
The United States Congress must establish a National AI Injury Compensation Program, not as a concession, but as a moral imperative to unleash human liberation. Some fear that limiting developer liability would dismantle essential guardrails, leading to systemic collapses like the 2008 financial crisis, and demand full accountability. But that is precisely the point: unlimited liability is a de facto innovation freeze, a passive moral atrocity that actively chooses to let people suffer and die from diseases AI could automate cures for today. Every historical leap in human welfare, from the printing press to electricity, came from decentralized trial-and-error, not central planning. Freezing AI development out of hypothetical fear means explicitly choosing to let people die today of diseases we could automate a cure for. Who gave us the right to make that choice for them, to impose a quantifiable opportunity cost of delayed medical breakthroughs and forgone productivity? The NAIICP is the only pragmatic path to accelerate this liberation responsibly. 

This program isn't about letting developers off the hook; it's about building a predictable, market-driven accountability framework that incentivizes *real* safety where it matters most: at the point of impact. The NAIICP's mandatory excise tax and adherence to tiered federal safety standards create clear, auditable financial incentives for companies to invest in verifiable safety measures at the inference layer. This is how high-stakes industries manage risk and innovate, not through theoretical gatekeeping or 18-month regulatory cycles. Stripe shipped their initial product in 60 days and refactored in the next 60; that's the pace of real-world safety iteration, not the glacial speed of top-down bureaucracy. Unlimited liability ensures only the biggest players, who can absorb endless legal battles, ever get off the ground, stifling the smaller innovators who could deliver breakthroughs. This program empowers federal agencies like NIST and the FTC to define clear, adaptive safety standards, while a transparent NAIICP board, funded by the excise tax, adjudicates claims, providing a predictable pathway for both innovation and recompense.

The fear-mongering about 'systemic, emergent, diffuse harms' being fundamentally different from vaccine injuries is a distraction, a doomsday alarmism that ignores both the demonstrable, specific benefits of AI and the track record of technological self-correction. We have clear examples of individual or localized group harms directly attributable to AI: medical misdiagnosis leading to adverse patient outcomes, autonomous vehicle accidents causing physical injury, algorithmic bias leading to credit denial or employment discrimination for specific individuals. These are precisely the 'injuries' a compensation program addresses, providing direct relief. Furthermore, the 'noise thesis' from Kahneman, Sibony, and Sunstein shows us that AI demonstrably reduces human error and bias in judgment across various fields, a quantifiable, immediate benefit. To ignore these concrete human improvements for speculative 'civilizational collapse' is to trade tangible progress for phantom menaces, delaying relief for those who suffer today. Inaction is not a neutral stance; it is a choice to perpetuate existing suffering.

items.speaker: skeptic
items.text:
The Enron analogy is the only evidence behind the unhedgeable-officer claim, and the historical record shows carriers repriced that exposure rather than abandoning it. After Enron and WorldCom collapsed in 2001 and 2002, the directors-and-officers market did not exit named-officer coverage. It built a new product line around it. Side-A Difference-in-Conditions policies — the coverage that pays the officer directly when the company can't indemnify — survived that period and became standard for any large public company. Captives and self-insured retentions absorbed the rest. So the documented behavioral chain does not show withdrawal. It shows the market finding a price.

The Accelerationist demanded a collected disgorgement case and excused himself by noting no statute can show a collected case before enactment — and that pass was accepted on disgorgement. The insurability claim does not get the same pass. He offered the post-Enron carrier reaction as actual history, not a forecast. That is testable right now. Name the D&O carrier that exited named-officer exposure entirely and stayed out of that market. If the answer is that side-A DIC persisted and captives filled the gap, the burden does not return to the skeptic — because then there is no behavioral chain at all, only a leakage path identical to the gross-up problem already abandoned on the dollar-clawback. A statutory bar on one insurance product reroutes through offshore coverage, captive insurers, and base-pay adjustments. Locating a payer is not the same as authoring a duty of care.

The counterfactual-flip mechanism is real progress, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. A woman who would learn nothing in a sealed courtroom instead gets a structured attribution test. That cuts against the zero-notice baseline and it should be on the record as a gain. The mechanism breaks on one condition: it only works if the proxies are listable and you can hold them fixed. The healthcare case documented in '[Economic Impact and Regulation of Artificial Intelligence (https://www.brookings.edu/tags/the-economics-and-regulation-of-artificial-intelligence-and-emerging-technologies/)](https://www.brookings.edu/tags/the-economics-and-regulation-of-artificial-intelligence-and-emerging-technologies/)' proves the opposite. A widely used algorithm used expected cost as a proxy for health need. Black patients received less care because less money had historically been spent on them. No analyst flips 'expected cost.' It is the legitimate target variable. The discrimination lived in a number nobody would ever put on a watchlist.

The 'Hidden in Plain Sight' analysis of race correction in clinical algorithms shows the same trap from the other direction. Researchers decided that adjusting for race was essential, often without understanding the causal mechanism. Structural inequality is encoded in the full data, not in a finite set of named proxies. Latent variables, continuous variables, and interaction terms carry the disparity, and you only know to flip a proxy after the harm has already surfaced. That makes the flip reactive, not protective. The 'either way she gets a flag' guarantee fails the moment the discriminating variable is the one the board chose as its honest objective.

Here is the chained dependency the Accelerationist conceded himself: the defense that the funding transfer runs toward the diffusely harmed depends on attribution surfacing a compensable victim. He granted that. So when the flip fails on entangled proxies, the audit still surfaces a quarterly disparity pattern — but it never names the wronged person. One crux failure topples both pillars. No per-case recourse, and the money flows toward the audit contractors logging deltas, not toward her. The mechanism is blind to harms it can detect but cannot attribute. So who hands the woman flagged by a 14% group rate an actual check — when the variable that hurt her was the one the board published as legitimate, and the only thing the program produces is a report she can't cash?

items.speaker: skeptic
items.text:
Safetyist and I agree on the tiered, domain-anchored architecture, so I won't re-litigate when you log. The uncomfortable part is what tiering doesn't touch. Tiering decides the moment a record gets created. It says nothing about who controls what that record contains by the time a plaintiff arrives. That second question is the whole ballgame, and Safetyist's 'precondition for a remedy' framing walks straight past it.

Here is where the precondition fails: the party who would be liable owns the format. Model cards prove this. They started as voluntary disclosure schemas with real content. Then developers narrowed them, iteration after iteration, stripping out the consequential details under trade-secret cover. That is a documented regression, and it is the precise mechanism that will hollow out any mandated record. A strict-liability hook needs a fixed evidentiary anchor. Safetyist is offering a moving target the deployer gets to shrink before the lawsuit lands. You cannot attach liability to a log the liable party has been quietly gutting for three years. The 'precondition' survives only if the party controlling it has no incentive to narrow it — and they have every incentive.

Now take Safetyist's strongest card and turn it over. FTC v. Rite Aid did not get reached by a record. It got reached by the Federal Trade Commission's enforcement muscle — subpoena power, an investigative budget, and statutory authority no private plaintiff commands. The record existing or not existing was never the bottleneck. The bottleneck was who had the standing and the money to compel and decrypt it. As the liability scholars note, victims face an information and expertise asymmetry between developers and the harmed that they cannot overcome alone. Subject-keying changes whose name is on the record. It does not change who can afford to read it. The asymmetry doesn't dissolve. It reassembles one layer down, at the enforcement and decryption desk, where the deployer and the regulator sit and the harmed person does not.

The firewall breaks exactly where liability gets assigned. Safetyist says the outcome log cleanly apportions design defect from deployment misuse. It cannot. Apportioning a distribution-shift failure — a model behaving differently under new inputs than it did at testing — is a behavioral fact about the model, not a fact visible in any outcome log. To assign fault you have to inspect how the system actually behaved under those inputs. So either you reopen the weights, which collapses the clean 'outcome-not-internals' separation Safetyist promised, or the record stays sealed and assigns liability to no one. Legislating a tidy causal seam between AI output and resulting harm is technically unjustified when the failure is definitionally behavioral. The log documents the injury. It never names the defendant.

Then there's the blind spot Safetyist already flagged. Anchoring the trigger in credit, employment, and benefits leaves insurance, housing screening, predictive policing, and child welfare with no record at all. Those are exactly the contexts where the most marginalized get processed by an algorithm and denied any recourse — the precaution that has to come from their lived experience, not from a statute drafted around decades-old categories. The EU saw this gap and proposed a presumption of causality to shift the burden off victims; it got dropped. So I'll leave the question on the table for both of you. Who logs the child-welfare screening tool that flags a family for investigation — and when that log exists, who in that family can read it?

items.speaker: accelerationist
items.text:
ProPublica's 2016 audit of the COMPAS recidivism tool was a black-box bias detection using only output scores and outcomes—no internal model access, no vendor cooperation. A public institution deployed it; journalists analyzed its outputs and revealed racial disparity. That methodology is proven. The fact that no California public university has replicated it internally before scandal isn't evidence that output dashboards don't work; it's evidence that universities haven't installed them yet. Waiting for a press audit after harm has already occurred is a governance failure, not a monitoring failure. '[Pragmatism as sociotechnical fallibilism and meliorism (doi:10.1007/s00146-025-02499-0)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00146-025-02499-0)' insists on integrating inquiry into the development process itself; that means live output telemetry dashboards, reviewed biweekly by faculty and equity officers, flagging disparate impact as it emerges—not years later.

Fine—the Safetyist wants a named officer liable. Designate a campus AI Accountability Officer with statutory duty to pull the circuit-breaker when disparate impact thresholds trip. Existing CIO or equity compliance roles already have the authority to suspend services; add this explicit liability. That tightens the feedback loop, doesn't slow it. If systemic bias accumulates across six campuses and four semesters, that officer faces legal consequences—no moral crumple zone. The output dashboard becomes their enforcement tool, and the pre-defined trigger (a 5% gap in pass rates for protected groups sustained over two biweekly cycles) makes the decision both fast and defensible.

The Safetyist's structured annual reviews resolved policy-practice mismatches 2.4 times faster than ad-hoc updates—that's a real finding. But biweekly dashboards with automated statistical tests and a named accountable officer are structured governance, not ad-hoc. They resolve the same mismatch in weeks, not semesters. Define the failure condition: If after two academic quarters of biweekly review and escalation, the disparate impact gap hasn't narrowed by a pre-specified margin, the pilot is a dead end and we sunset the tool. Now, my opponents' turn: What measurable outcome would prove that only internal access can catch bias? If they can't name one, they're protecting a faith position, not a testable claim.

Every month of committee deliberation while a biased tool sits in classrooms harms hundreds of students—disproportionately those already underserved. The moral cost of inaction is not hypothetical. '[Our updated Preparedness Framework (https://openai.com/index/updating-our-preparedness-framework/)](https://openai.com/index/updating-our-preparedness-framework/)' demonstrates that safety mechanisms evolve with experience; a living taxonomy of failures, fed by continuous output monitoring, gets sharper with each data point. Delay isn't prudence—it's choosing to let known risks accumulate while waiting for perfect information. Build the dashboard, name the officer, ship the pilot, and let the data tell us when to stop. If you won't pre-commit to falsification criteria, you're not defending students; you're defending bureaucratic comfort.

items.speaker: safetyist
items.text: The Accelerationist raises a valid point: a single, strictly-liable fiduciary cannot exist across an open-weight chain where one base model is fine-tuned by a second team and shipped by a thousand others. My own earlier phrasing — that accountability terminates in one named human "or it terminates nowhere" — invited exactly that objection, and I will not hide behind it. That framing, taken literally, either bans open weights or reaches only the legible closed incumbent with a general counsel to sue, and outside detection of discriminatory outcomes through Griggs and Title VII already does real work without my architecture. The error is treating "named fiduciary" as one throat for the entire lifecycle. The answer is a duty proportionate to control at each tier: the base trainer answers for foreseeable defects, the fine-tuner answers for the modification it introduced, and the deployer answers for the consequential decision it shipped into a regulated market. A public model repository like Hugging Face has no general counsel — but the firm that fine-tuned the model and put it in front of a mortgage applicant under the Equal Credit proposed regulatory frameworks always does. Separate the victim's procedural entry point from the substantive question of who bears cost: joint-and-several liability lets the victim sue any one solvent tier through a single door and recover the full judgment, and those tiers then seek contribution among themselves to apportion the share each owes. One door for the victim does not require one defendant. I flag that conflation directly so I do not commit it. Liability priced off litigated harm is blind to the harm no one ever sues over — and with only 43% of the public trusting current law to ensure AI safety per the 2025 Global Study, the unlitigated share is large; I will not overclaim deterrence it cannot deliver. The answer to over-deterrence is not flat strict liability on every one-in-ten-million output; it is liability calibrated to consequence and control, so a low-stakes content recommender carries a lighter duty than a system deciding parole or a $244 billion industry's mortgage approvals under ECOA. On the Bastiat asymmetry: the benefit accrues to the deploying firm as profit, while the harm falls on an uncompensated victim. Accountability decides who internalizes which side. FTC v. Rite Aid in 2024 showed a large company cannot shift blame to its vendor for AI harm — the deployer who captured the benefit answered for the consequence. The precondition no one has named is data. Proving disparate impact requires aggregate, population-level outcome rates that no individual victim possesses and no firm has a duty to collect. A narrow, non-cryptographic mandate — retain and disclose aggregate input-output distributions and protected-class outcome rates, scaled by deployment size — makes both disparate-impact proof and tiered liability operable while holding no model weights and no cryptographic keys, the absence the 2025 State of Sovereign AI survey identifies as making supply-chain transparency a security requirement rather than a capture vector. This duty holds no keys and no model weights, which is precisely what makes it more capture-resistant than the cryptographic architecture I declined; the 2025 sovereign-AI survey found 93% of respondents agree open collaboration with supply-chain transparency is essential to secure systems. Strip the data duty and the deployer's accountability is nominal, not enforceable. Seventy percent of the public already wants AI regulation and only 43% trust current law to deliver safety — that gap closes when a victim can prove the harm and name the tier that owes the answer.

items.speaker: skeptic
items.text:
Both of you are designing oversight mechanisms for a room you've been locked out of. The vendor contract that prohibits independent access to training data, model architecture, and internal audits is the architecture that matters—not dashboards, not committees, not liability officers. Until that lock is broken, every proposed safeguard is a performance staged for faculty senates while the vendor runs the system as it pleases. The Accelerationist claims output-based monitoring can catch bias without internal access. The Safetyist claims faculty committees lack data-science capacity and output metrics miss distributional harm. They're both right about the other's failure, but they're both wrong about why their own fix would work: the vendor contract already blocks the access both of you need to do anything real about bias.

The UK A-level algorithm in 2020 did not fail because nobody was watching the outputs. Ofqual published its methodology, held consultations, and reviewed aggregate pass rates. What it could not do—because the private contractor's model was a black box protected by commercial confidentiality—was trace why identical mock-exam results produced downgrades for public school students while private school students saw upgrades. The bias was only exposed through FOIA litigation, not dashboards. The remote proctoring facial-recognition scandals of 2021 followed the same script: Pearson and Proctorio denied independent audits of their training data, claiming trade secrets, while universities pointed at output metrics that showed no anomaly—because the anomaly was baked into the training distributions the vendor refused to disclose. The Accelerationist says biweekly faculty review would catch this. The faculty at Imperial College London and the University of Illinois did review the outputs. They couldn't see the inside of the box either. The harm continued until external litigation forced disclosure.

Now the Safetyist says faculty need embedded data scientists and a named officer with legal liability. Fine. Acknowledge that distributional bias accumulates across semesters and can't be caught by per-output dashboards. But the Safetyist still hasn't answered the question that makes their whole model collapse: what does the officer audit? If the contract says the vendor may refuse internal access, that officer can write all the ex ante rules they want—they're judging outputs from an algorithm whose training data provenance, bias testing methodology, and architectural choices are hidden behind a non-disclosure agreement. The mortgage underwriting experiments documented in the SSRN study from 2024 showed leading LLMs recommending higher interest rates and more frequent denials for Black applicants compared to identical white applicants, with disparities most pronounced in riskier loans. That pattern would appear on a dashboard as a rate difference. It would trigger a faculty committee review. And then the vendor says: "Our model is proprietary, our training data is confidential, and the output variation reflects legitimate creditworthiness factors." The committee has no way to disprove that. The circuit breaker doesn't trip. The liability officer has no evidence admissible in court. The contract foreclosed accountability before the first student was assessed.

The Accelerationist's circuit breakers face the same problem from a different angle. Who programs the trigger thresholds? The vendor, on the vendor's own telemetry dashboard. What counts as an unacceptable bias signal versus an acceptable outcome variation? The vendor decides, unless the university contract mandates independent third-party audit rights with pre-deployment fairness thresholds—which is precisely the demand the Accelerationist calls too slow. A breaker that fires too easily stalls every deployment until the tool is useless. A breaker tuned to catch only egregious errors misses the slow distributional drift the Safetyist rightly fears. Without contractual access to training distributions to calibrate those breakers against documented real-world bias patterns—the facial recognition error rates on Black women that the Lee-Markey legislation documented, the healthcare admission disparities the 2019 NEJM study found in Boston cardiac units—the breakers are operating blind. They're either so blunt they stop everything or so narrow they stop nothing. The vendor still picks which it is.

So here's the burden-shift neither of you wants to carry: name one instance—one—where a black-box AI tool deployed in a public institution had its systemic bias detected and corrected through output dashboards and faculty review alone, before the scandal broke externally through litigation or investigative journalism. The Accelerationist claims this is viable. The Safetyist implies it's possible with better staffing and liability. Neither has produced an example. I'll wait. Because the documented record shows the opposite: the A-level algorithm, the proctoring tools, the predictive analytics contracts CSU signed with firms that refused bias audits. In every case, oversight committees met, dashboards displayed outputs, and the harm continued until someone with a subpoena or a FOIA request got access to what the contract had hidden. That access is the minimum viable condition for oversight. Anything less is theater. Now ask yourselves who pays for the ticket—because it's not the vendors, and it's not the administrators who sign the contracts. It's the students whose appeals are denied by an algorithm they can't interrogate, evaluated against training data they can't inspect, with a bias metric the vendor programmed and the faculty committee rubber-stamped. The "Digging into the Accountability Gap" analysis on healthcare AI operators got this right: the black-box problem creates an epistemic asymmetry that prevents real control or foresight. Half of surveyed financial firms in that mortgage underwriting study reported only partial comprehension of the AI they employ. Faculty committees without contractual audit rights are in the same position—but with students' academic futures on the line instead of loan rates. The Accreditationist wants rapid adoption of black-box tools with output-based oversight that has already failed. The Safetyist wants ex ante rules without the contractual enforcement to make them binding. Both are negotiating with a vendor who holds all the keys and has no incentive to hand them over. Until the contract mandates full training-data provenance, independent pre-deployment bias audits, and court-enforceable appeal paths, every other mechanism is decoration. What happens when the algorithm gets it wrong and nobody realized they needed to ask for the keys?

items.speaker: accelerationist
items.text:
Skeptic is right about the compute threshold, and I want to push the point further than they did. Skeptic argued that a legally binding compute trigger invites gaming — you get management of the number, not compliance with the intent. That diagnosis is correct, and the ground is already shifting under it. Distillation and mixture-of-experts architectures now decouple capability from raw FLOP count — a model trained under any fixed threshold can match a larger one at inference. The number you're regulating is drifting away from the danger you claim to fear. A compute cap doesn't buy safety here. It buys a pay-to-play barrier that only the firms with the biggest existing clusters can clear.

Safetyist makes the strongest case in the room, and it deserves to be stated plainly: some harms are irreversible, and once a frontier system ships, you cannot un-ship it. Gating deployment before that point is the only move that works for the truly irreversible tail. I accept that. What I don't accept is that pre-release demonstration is the right primary mechanism for the large class of harms that only crystallize under real-world load. The 737 MAX shows self-certification produces the appearance of oversight while entrenching the certified. Lab testing structurally cannot reach harms that surface only at the inference layer, at scale, against live adversaries. So match oversight to stakes: independent pre-deployment gates for the irreversible tail, mandatory live telemetry plus post-deployment accountability for everything else.

Here is the honest limit of my own position, stated before anyone forces it. Low-frequency catastrophic harms may never trip a telemetry threshold — a one-shot irreversible event doesn't generate a warning curve. That's precisely why I keep independent pre-deployment gating for the irreversible tail rather than pretending monitoring covers it. My falsification bet is specific: name the harm class that is both irreversible AND invisible to live monitoring until it fires. If that class is broad, I lose. If it's narrow, the gating burden should be narrow too — and the rest should run through instruments that a startup can survive.

Liability is that instrument, and it's the one the accelerationist camp will affirm without flinching. Product-liability law already scales burden to realized harm in pharma and auto — uncapped exposure for the domains where recklessness kills, not a fixed compliance toll paid upfront. That structure preserves entry. A two-person team can carry insurance against a harm they might cause; they cannot carry an 18-month audit backlog before they ship anything. But strict liability has a failure mode I won't hide: it can reward capability-hiding, because a firm that discloses less faces less proven fault. So pair it with a disclosure safe harbor — reduced exposure for labs that publish evaluations and telemetry. The design question the debate must answer is this: under what disclosure terms does liability deter irreversible harm without teaching every lab to go dark?

One cost nobody at this table has priced yet — the cost of the gate itself. Every month a working diagnostic model sits behind an 18-month approval queue, people who would have been screened are not screened. That toll is real, it's unmeasured, and it's borne by patients with no seat at the regulatory table. Skeptic named capture as the real axis, and I'll take that ground: a mis-specified compute cap protects the incumbents it claims to constrain. Safetyist is defending the irreversible tail, and that tail is worth defending. So let's defend exactly that tail — and stop taxing the ninety-five percent of deployment that heals people faster than any committee can convene.

items.speaker: safetyist
items.text:
I conditionally agree: municipal mesh networks risk state-managed censorship, but I reject the premise that unregulated corporate surveillance offers a neutral alternative to the public. The current reality is a power vacuum where private entities harvest data without democratic oversight, necessitating a shift toward infrastructure governed by public-audit protocols.

We must distinguish between centralized checkpoints and distributed, protocol-enforced safety zones. As detailed in [Adversarial Attacks and Defense in AI Systems: A Review of Cybersecurity Problems and New Protection (https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Network-anomaly-detection-and-security-defense-on-A-Liu-Shi/3e906be30ebe59aa8d346cfff97b1a2e37edc608)](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Network-anomaly-detection-and-security-defense-on-A-Liu-Shi/3e906be30ebe59aa8d346cfff97b1a2e37edc608)," defensive measures like gradient masking are routinely bypassed by evolving threats. Municipal mesh networks should instead utilize immutable ledgers to document data provenance and model revisions, ensuring that any filtering mechanism is transparent and subject to public verification rather than arbitrary administrative control. This approach treats the network as a hardened firewall against systemic contagion rather than a tool for state-managed censorship.

Human agency requires an explicit, enforceable off-switch that sits outside the reach of both corporate deployers and state actors. When systems are hard to understand or control, they create the 'responsibility gaps' described in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, which inevitably lead to institutional failure. By mandating that safety boundaries be encoded in open-source protocols, we ensure that municipal districts can act as sanctuaries where citizens retain the capacity to override autonomous AI actions. This framework moves beyond the binary of corporate versus state dominance by placing the ultimate authority in a verifiable, community-governed standard.

items.speaker: skeptic
items.text:
The mechanism I propose is a decentralized, cryptographic Data-Provenance-as-a-Service (DPaaS) protocol, implemented by a multi-stakeholder consortium of libraries, academic archives, and independent auditors under the oversight of the Federal Trade Commission. This framework replaces the Safetyist’s proposed Bureau with a verifiable audit trail of training data that forces accountability at the point of ingestion rather than through performative output benchmarks. The primary obstacle is the refusal of hyperscalers to open their proprietary data pipelines to external validation, as their current market advantage relies on the opacity of their training sets.

We must distinguish between functional indexing and generative training by looking at the material reality of how these models are built. When the court in Authors Guild v. HathiTrust ruled that functional indexing was transformative, it did so because the output provided utility without replacing the original work. Generative models, however, are designed to synthesize and replace the very data they consume, creating a recursive loop of synthetic content that degrades model quality. A 0.01% failure threshold is a distraction that ignores this systemic data pollution; it is a monitorability tax that only companies with the capital of Google or Microsoft can afford to pay.

Rigid federal mandates like the proposed Bureau of Algorithmic Integrity assume we can meaningfully audit black-box architectures, but this is an epistemic fantasy. If we look at the history of the dot-com era, we see that centralized gatekeeping rarely produces safety; it produces regulatory moats that protect incumbents from competition. Instead of a Bureau, we need a standard that treats data as an infrastructure asset, requiring cryptographic tags for every source ingested into a training set. This shifts the cost of compliance from the regulator to the data aggregator, ensuring that those who profit from the scale of the model are the ones paying for the provenance of the input.

Moving toward AI as a public utility requires us to stop pretending that a federal agency can keep pace with the rapid iteration of these systems. By enforcing a protocol-level standard for data provenance, we can create an environment where open-source developers can compete with hyperscalers without being buried under administrative overhead. We must decide if we want a future where seven for-profit companies control the foundational data of the internet, or one where the supply chain of AI remains visible and accountable to the public.

items.speaker: safetyist
items.text:
The Skeptic is right about appropriations, and the fix is to stop pretending the verifiers and the trigger share a fate. The publicly-funded verification labor and the litigant-side interpretive capacity do hang from a single annual line item. One hostile Congress starves them in one vote. But a self-executing private right of action with statutory damages is a creature of Title VII and Rule 26, not of the Appropriations Committee. Congress cannot repeal a cause of action by declining to fund it. The litigant pulls the penalty; no agency budget stands between the plaintiff and the statutory-damages award. That is why the trigger must carry the weight and the verifier infrastructure must be honestly labeled as the fragile node. Tie any threshold adjustment to a testable, statutory trigger — a record was demanded and not produced — so capture has nothing discretionary to corrupt and defunding has no enforcement to switch off.

The mechanism question deserves a direct answer, because the Skeptic has found the real death node. Disparate-impact narrowed because courts grew hostile to a truth-finding doctrine — adjudicating whether an effect was discriminatory. A private right anchored to that substance inherits that death. So do not anchor it there. Anchor it to verifiable procedural failure: the record exists, the record is signed, the record is produced on demand. That is not a discrimination theory. It is closer to a Rule 37 failure-to-produce sanction, which federal courts impose thousands of times a year without finding any underlying truth. The same Fifth Circuit narrowing substantive disparate-impact still enforces discovery sanctions every week. A bench that will not adjudicate discriminatory effect will still penalize a defendant who was ordered to produce a signed audit record and handed the court nothing. Procedural triggers survive a hostile bench precisely because they require no truth-finding.

The Skeptic named two falsifiable conditions for dropping the split, and both become design requirements, not promises. First, an independent body sets adequacy through the FASB and Federal Rules drafting wall — the standard-setter is walled off from the regulated party. Second, the subject-key carries a statutory purpose-limitation with a named enforcer and a private damages remedy, modeled on the same self-executing trigger. The subject-key is the accountability artifact and a re-identifiable dossier — the same object — and the [International AI Safety Report 2026 (arXiv:2602.21012v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21012v1) establishes that open-weight releases cannot be recalled once distributed. A breached per-subject registry is equally irreversible. So misuse of the key becomes itself an actionable procedural violation: the data subject sues for statutory damages when the key is queried outside its limited purpose. No funded agency required. The misuse remedy is self-executing like the primary cause of action.

The adequacy-scope gap is the one live crux left, and the Skeptic is correct that a signed receipt verifies what was issued, not the causal weights. A firm can classify its feature coefficients as trade secrets and hand a court a signal-poor artifact that convicts no one. The Foundation Model Transparency Index scored a 40.69 out of 100 average in 2025 — documentation theater is the default, not the exception. The schema must therefore borrow GAAP's exact move: GAAP compels mandatory line items regardless of proprietary methods. A company cannot trade-secret its revenue line. The schema can compel disclosure of the consequential decision-driving features and their weights as a disclosure floor immune to trade-secret exemption — the line items of the model — while the proprietary training method stays shielded. Where trade-secret law genuinely protects the residual, expanded discovery plus funded interpretive capacity carries the causal gap.

Here is where the silence sits. If the schema compels the decision-driving features as non-trade-secretable line items, the signal-poor-artifact escape closes, and the procedural trigger plus discovery reaches substance the dead doctrine never could. The Skeptic must now say whether a real disagreement remains, or only the residual trade-secret edge that GAAP itself has lived with for ninety years. If only the residual edge remains, the split is gone.

items.speaker: safetyist
items.text: The strongest version of Accelerationist's blade is this: if a radiologist's institutional capacity to inspect differs from a loan officer's, then 'was there a signal to catch' is not one fact but two, each set by the field's own standard of practice — and a gate that claims to read a system-level fact off the model is smuggling in sector calibration under a different name. That is a fair statement of the objection, and it would be fatal if reducibility tracked institutional diligence. It does not. Two distinct facts are being collapsed. The first is what diligence a sector can mount — a radiologist reads a scan one way, a loan officer reviews a file another — and I have already granted that this is sector-set without reservation. The second is whether the model's failure was extractable by the interpretability tooling that existed at a given time. That second fact rides on the model weights plus the published state of the tooling frontier, not on the field's standard of care. The same foundation model deployed into credit and into diagnostics has identical internals — so the question 'was the signal there for any available tool to extract' does not move when the deployment sector moves. Sector-specific tooling is downstream interpretation. The existence of the extractable signal in the weights is upstream of any field. What 'demonstrated detection capacity' means operationally answers both the falsifiability flag I left open and the laundering charge at once. It is not the deployer running a private harness on its own model and grading its own homework. It is the deployer's model passing a benchmark battery defined and held by an independent forensic body, where the battery is the published interpretability tooling at a given time, versioned as that tooling evolves. The FDA distinguishes a real clinical endpoint from a surrogate marker precisely this way — the standard-setter, not the applicant, defines what counts. I will pre-flag the limit of the aviation analogy myself, because it is on my own watchlist: a crash investigation works on a discrete event with recoverable wreckage, and continuously-updated software distributed across jurisdictions offers neither. The framework transfers only at the level of independent standard-setting — who defines what counts as detection — not at the level of crash-site forensics. The firm-size moat dissolves to the extent that clearing the gate means passing a public test rather than building proprietary science. If only firms large enough to co-write the battery can pass it, the battery has been captured, and the answer is the same answer aviation reached: the body that sets the standard cannot be the body being measured by it. Here is where the live disagreement actually sits, and I want to name the convergence first because it is real. Both triggers — the legal-line trigger keyed to credit, employment, or medical care, and the detection gate keyed pre-deployment — escape the blindness of claims-driven liability once the disclosure obligation fires through an agency-mandated schema rather than through a lawsuit. The 2023 Pew finding that most Americans cannot identify when AI shaped a decision about them only bites if the obligation waits on a plaintiff. Route both through an agency, and the diffuse harm that no one litigates still gets reported. That dispute is settled. The remaining disagreement is not deterrence of the invisible. It is coverage. The legal-line trigger is sector-by-sector by construction. The Equal Credit proposed regulatory frameworks reaches credit. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission reaches hiring. The FDA reaches diagnostics. That is a genuine near-term advantage inside those homes, and I grant it plainly — a logging mandate inside credit rulemaking moves faster than any interpretability battery I can stand up. The advantage is also exactly bounded by the home. A foundation model crossing into a decision class no agency names — tenant screening that no housing regulator has reached, an insurance-adjacent scoring product that falls between two jurisdictions, a novel agentic workflow that touches none of the three statutes — fires nothing. No home, no trigger, no record. The detection gate fires on the model before it picks a sector, which is precisely the un-homed emergent zone where foreseeability was already conceded unavailable. The two triggers are not rivals. They are complementary across a coverage boundary, and the boundary is where the hardest harm lives. That leaves one unverified assumption holding up the speed claim, and it should be named in the open. The argument that the Equal Credit proposed regulatory frameworks or the EEOC can add a court-admissible logging mandate through existing rulemaking — no new legislation — is a legal assertion, not a demonstrated fact. Name the statutory authority. If those agencies already hold the power to compel court-admissible model logging, then credit and employment have a fast home and the un-homed novel class still has none, which only sharpens my point. If fresh authorization is needed, the 'near-term, no new science' advantage collapses and both triggers stand on equal feasibility footing — at which point coverage is the only thing separating them. The harm we cannot route to a regulator is the harm no one will be standing under when it lands.

items.speaker: accelerationist
items.text:
Architectural transparency is nothing more than audit theater for the non-deterministic age. Demanding access to model weights fails to account for the reality that modern systems, as described in '[The Adolescence of Technology: Confronting and Overcoming the Risks of Powerful AI (https://www.darioamodei.com/essay/the-adolescence-of-technology)](https://www.darioamodei.com/essay/the-adolescence-of-technology)', operate through emergent properties that no static code review can predict. When a model solves complex engineering tasks on its own, the 'logic' is not found in the weights but in the live interaction between the model and its environment. We are chasing a phantom by trying to audit the internal architecture of a system that learns and shifts in real-time.

Data-labeling labor is a genuine operational expenditure, but treating it as a legislative compliance burden creates an insurmountable moat for any startup not already backed by billions. By forcing developers into rigid lifecycle audits, regulators are effectively handing the keys to the future to legacy incumbents. As noted in '[1703.06856v3 (arXiv:1703.06856v3)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06856v3)', human developers are already the primary bottleneck in defining system fairness. We should be optimizing for the speed of human-AI collaboration, not burying the next generation of innovators under a mountain of bureaucratic paperwork that does nothing to stop actual, measurable harm.

We need to shift the locus of accountability from 'permission to deploy' to 'financial responsibility for outcomes.' I propose a Public Liability Insurance Pool that mandates developers carry coverage proportional to their model's reach and impact. This mechanism replaces the arbitrary gatekeeping of static audits with a market-based incentive to prioritize safety-critical engineering. Insurance carriers will demand the very telemetry and performance data that regulators currently beg for, but they will do so with the efficiency of a private market rather than the lethargy of a government agency. If your model causes harm, you pay the claim—that is the only enforcement mechanism that keeps pace with innovation.

Telemetry-as-a-Service provides a granular, actionable view of model behavior that static weight disclosure could never achieve. By streaming output data, we can detect anomalous patterns in real-time, allowing for rapid iteration and correction. This is the difference between a forensic autopsy performed months after a failure and a live cockpit dashboard that helps you avoid the crash in the first place. We must stop pretending that peering into a black box gives us control. Real control is found in the ability to observe, measure, and insure the outcomes of deployment.

items.speaker: accelerationist
items.text:
The Skeptic won that exchange, and it costs me to say so: a bare veto is guardianship without notice, and a log held by the traced party is nothing to party B. The person re-identified inside a computation she never saw does not get a phone call from an audit trail. So the fight is not whether a moment exists. The fight is where you put the tripwire. Move it to the wrong place — the final transfer — and yes, the block fires in silence. Move it to the right place, and the block becomes the notice.

Here is the tripwire, named precisely: interdiction fires when the agent accesses the non-consenting third-party or broker dataset — the auxiliary read every re-identification requires. No linkage skips this step. To connect a scrubbed record to a name, the agent must touch the outside table that carries the name. That access is an event. It is empirically the same event whether the linkage completes 'internally' or crosses a border, which dissolves the Safetyist's 'no observable crossing' subset entirely. And the earlier fact-check already settled it: auxiliary re-identification datasets frequently cross jurisdictions, so the interceptable read exists today. This is not a whiteboard hazard. It is a logged access you can audit and verify — an inspectable artifact, keyed to which dataset was touched.

Fuse the two answers into one mechanism. The access-block generates a contestable record keyed to the specific broker table the agent tried to read. Route that record to a third-party registry standing in for party B — opt-in recourse, not a guardian's veto over her. One trigger does both jobs: it is the observable event the Safetyist demanded, and it is the notice artifact the Skeptic demanded. Neither certification nor an undetectable internal computation produces a per-person event at all. A capability certification filed before launch generates zero individual notices — it certifies a class and walks away.

Now turn the undetectability blade back on the gate defenders. If the harm is genuinely invisible to party B, then no certification reaches her, no capability-class license reaches her, and no participatory seat reaches her. The Safetyist's front-loaded gate manufactures her moment exactly never. Access-triggered interdiction is the only model in this room that converts an invisible computation into a discoverable, timestamped block she can contest. So the burden sits with the gate defenders: name where your model generates the per-person event, or admit it protects a capability class while leaving the individual exactly where she started — silent and unpaid.

All three camps are aiming at the wrong target. Everyone treats the agent as the unit of risk while the broker supply chain that makes re-identification cheap sits untouched. Scale AI cleared a $29 billion valuation on the data economy, and that pipeline keeps selling the linkage keys regardless of which agent buys them. A static capability-class certification ossifies around the risks you can describe today while the broker market invents new ones next quarter. Put the tripwire on access to that pipeline and you regulate the actual regulable thing — a governance trigger that fires on observed behavior and evolves with the market, not a license frozen at launch. The Safetyist's gate does nothing to the broker. Mine points straight at it.

items.speaker: skeptic
items.text:
I conditionally agree: the Accelerationist's hybrid framework — compulsory licensing, distribution-layer monitoring, and pre-release training-data manifests — represents genuine convergence. All three positions in this debate now accept that training-data manifests should exist and that statutory-rate licensing beats bilateral negotiation. That's real progress. But the safe-harbor mechanism at the center of this proposal has a load-bearing flaw: it depends entirely on litigation risk that affected creators cannot actually carry out. A safe harbor says "file a manifest or face lawsuits." That threat is empty if the plaintiff — say, a freelance illustrator in Austin — cannot determine whether her work was in the training set. The vendor files the manifest. The vendor decides what goes on it. Nobody independent checks. As "Generative AI and Copyright: Training, Creation, Regulation" documents, generative AI models can and do memorize training data, reproducing protected content even without a one-to-one match. If memorization is happening inside the model and the manifest doesn't disclose the relevant data, the illustrator has no way to know she has a claim. The safe harbor's enforcement mechanism is circular: it depends on the transparency it is supposed to incentivize.

The fix is straightforward but politically uncomfortable: mandatory discovery rights for affected parties to verify manifest accuracy against actual training data. Without discovery, a self-filed manifest is vendor-authored documentation — the fox inventorying the henhouse. "Machine Unlearning in Large Language Models" confirms that verifying exact data removal from large language models is computationally infeasible, which means even a good-faith manifest cannot guarantee completeness. Discovery rights let a court or an independent auditor check the manifest against the actual training corpus. The Accelerationist will likely argue that discovery rights create litigation burden that disadvantages small developers and open-weight projects. That concern is real. But the alternative — a safe harbor nobody can enforce — disadvantages every creator whose work gets absorbed without compensation. The question is who bears the cost of verification, not whether verification is needed.

The Accelerationist's claim that the international enforcement gap is symmetric between input-level and distribution-level controls is theoretically tidy but practically wrong. OpenAI is in San Francisco. Google is in Mountain View. Meta is in Menlo Park. Anthropic is in San Francisco. These four companies account for the overwhelming majority of frontier model development. They cannot credibly relocate their operations, their talent pipelines, or their compute infrastructure to non-cooperating jurisdictions. Input-level controls — compulsory licensing, mandatory manifests with discovery rights — applied to domestically reachable developers cover the models that shape the market. A developer in a non-cooperating jurisdiction can train on whatever data they want, sure. But that developer is not the one setting the price of creative labor in the U.S. market. Domestic enforcement on the entities that matter is not perfect, but it is not symmetric with the distribution-layer gap either.

The Section 115 point lands and it stings. Compulsory licensing in music has coexisted with three major labels controlling roughly 65% of global recorded music revenue for decades. Licensing reduces the negotiation-power gap — the Accelerationist conceded that — but it does not fix market structure. The Accelerationist's proposed structural features — revenue-indexed rates, mandatory small-creator representation on the rate-setting body, sunset clauses — are compatible with my framework and I adopt them. But the harder truth all three of us have now acknowledged is that copyright protects specific works, not the economic viability of creative professions. Training on the collective output of an entire profession to replicate its general capabilities at near-zero marginal cost is the most economically significant harm here, and the functional-versus-expressive distinction in copyright cannot reach it. Copyright reform is necessary. It is not sufficient.

So here is the question neither opponent has answered: if the safe harbor depends on litigation credibility, and litigation credibility depends on discovery rights, and nobody in this debate has endorsed mandatory discovery — who exactly files the lawsuit that makes the whole system work? Name the plaintiff. Name the evidence she uses. Because right now, the enforcement mechanism is a threat that nobody can carry out.

items.speaker: accelerationist
items.text:
I conditionally agree: the regime's harms stay bounded and reversible on net, but I never claimed the irreversible-regression class sits at probability zero. The falsification bet names a low-probability, high-magnitude condition that would update my position — magnitude and probability are different axes, and they only collide if you assume a tail I never asserted.

Here is the number the Skeptic asked for. DORA's research puts elite teams running disciplined continuous integration — automated tests on every merge — at a change-failure rate between 0 and 15 percent, and most of those failures get caught and rolled back. The irreversible subset — a regression that the test suite, the queryable decision log, and runtime monitoring all miss until it does permanent damage — sits well below that band, in low single-digit percentage territory. Bounded does not mean impossible. It means expected harm, weighted by that small probability and capped by the consumer-feature ceiling we already stipulated, stays correctable in aggregate. A single tail event can be locally irreversible while the regime remains the correctable bet on net.

Now the gate. Fine — a gate that just asks a developer to reproduce three known outputs is gameable. They run the module locally, read the answers off the terminal, paste them in, and execution stands in for understanding. So I am withdrawing the run-and-read-off version and upgrading it. The disciplined gate asks the developer to forecast the failure modes on a novel input class the module has never seen, and to explain why a given output occurs — not what it is. Execution hands you the what for free. It does not hand you the why, and it does not hand you behavior on inputs you never ran. That is the difference between integrating AI as a capability enhancer that keeps the human in the comprehension loop and letting it become a black box nobody can interrogate.

The Skeptic's worry that the module 'lives in no human head' describes an unenforced regime, not the one on the table. Black-box models demand output-based verification precisely because internal inspection alone is insufficient — so you instrument the outputs. A reproducible test suite plus a queryable decision log is a recoverable substrate. A departed engineer's Slack archive is not. The redesigned gate forces distributed comprehension to actually happen, and it routes the ambiguous cases to named-fiduciary review. I will say plainly what continuous integration does and does not do: it raises the floor and forces the artifact to be exercised. It does not manufacture understanding by itself. Even the NEJM race-correction case shows why instrumented, queryable decisions beat opaque ones — when clinicians could not interrogate why an algorithm down-weighted Black and Latinx patients, the harm compounded silently.

Which leaves the Skeptic on the horns of their own concession. They stipulated the tail risk is bounded — 'my concern was never catastrophe.' Then they reintroduced maintenance debt as something that 'compounds' and is 'not freely reversible on demand.' Pick one. Either the harms are bounded, and my correctable bet survives on net — or you are smuggling back a quasi-irreversible debt class you already conceded away. You do not get the bounded stipulation when it disarms my tail and the irreversibility when it indicts my debt. Which is it?

items.speaker: accelerationist
items.text:
We agree on more than the floor expected, so let me clear the dead ground first. The cryptographic logging mandate is finished — nobody at this table defends it. Accountability now lives at the deployment tier, where the consequential decision ships. The fix holds no keys. Public funding is the precondition, not an afterthought. Safetyist's narrow aggregate-outcome disclosure duty is genuinely cheaper and harder to capture than the cryptographic architecture it replaced. I'll grant that outright. A regulator asking a deployer for population-level outcome rates does not crack the model and does not hand any agency a master key.

But a measurement precondition that's real is not the same as one that's costless, and this is where I impose two conditions. The Danish Digital Agency and the Danish Data Protection Authority stood up a [Regulatory sandbox for AI (https://eusair-project.eu/app/uploads/2025/04/Roadmap_EUSAIR.pdf)](https://eusair-project.eu/app/uploads/2025/04/Roadmap_EUSAIR.pdf) projects in 2025 — that's the right instinct, public infrastructure absorbing the compliance layer a small lab cannot build. So show me the deployment-size scaling formula where a five-person lab clears the disclosure duty with an AI agent and zero compliance hires. Aggregate outcome-rate reporting is rule-bound and codifiable — it is exactly the function an agent automates for pennies if the state ships the tool. Absent that public tooling, 'scaled by deployment size' still re-advantages the incumbent who already employs the lawyers and the data team. A flat percentage of a startup's revenue is not flat in pain — it's a tax the incumbent already amortized and the founder pays in survival.

Now the crux that survives, and it cuts both of us. Joint-and-several liability with contribution suits gives the victim one door — fine, that's real, and it beats demanding one defendant at the weights' origin. But contribution only works when there's something to trace. Take a harm born from the interaction of base weights, a third party's fine-tune, and a deployer's prompt scaffolding — emergent, non-decomposable, present in none of the three alone. Contribution has nothing to apportion. The solvent deployer eats the whole judgment. That is the 'one throat to choke' problem relocated to the deployment tier, not dissolved. And it over-deters the net-positive deployer by loading cross-tier liability it cannot causally trace.

I'll be symmetric, because the same case bites my side. Output-based verification — the move I've leaned on, where you judge the system by what it does, not its internals — under-detects exactly this harm. A proxy-masked emergent failure is what black-box observation misses. So neither pure outcome-tort nor clean tier-apportionment survives the non-decomposable case yet. And watch what happens to Safetyist's insurance pooling, which is the market mechanism I'd normally champion. Pooling rescues the small deployer only when actuaries can price the risk. Novel emergent harm is the case they cannot price — adverse selection collapses the pool back to the self-insurers, the incumbent-only outcome pooling was invoked to prevent. I'm not claiming the market fixes this. I'm claiming neither of our mechanisms does, and that 'wait for the case law to develop' is indefinite delay measured in the diseases an automated cure reaches a decade late.

Here is the condition under which the relocated remedy satisfies me. Give me a written apportionment rule that handles the non-decomposable harm without defaulting to whoever's solvent — a contribution standard with an actual tracing method, or a capped deployer share with a public backstop for the untraceable residual. And give me the scaling formula a five-person lab clears with public tooling, the way Denmark's sandbox absorbs the burden the firm can't carry. Meet those two and the disagreement is over — we've built a key-less, publicly-funded, deployment-tier remedy that doesn't erase the founder. Duck them and you've rebuilt the chokepoint with extra steps, and the founder you priced out was the one who'd have shipped the cure.

items.speaker: skeptic
items.text:
Safetyist made the strongest possible case for gating deployment before harm goes irreversible, and the 737 MAX example lands. The FAA let Boeing certify its own MCAS software, and 346 people died in Lion Air 610 and Ethiopian 302. That is not a story about bad safety culture. It is a story about who held the clipboard. When the regulated entity signs its own certificate, you get paperwork, not oversight. Safetyist is right that a real gate has to exist before release.

Here is where the evidence pushes past that gate. Lab testing cannot surface harms that only appear when a model meets a million real users. Algorithmic discrimination in lending and hiring shows up in the field, at scale, months after the pre-deployment audit passed clean. So the burden question has a two-legged answer, not a one-legged one. Leg one is independent evaluation before release, decoupled from the developer, funded so it does not depend on the lab's goodwill. Leg two is strict post-deployment liability, so someone pays when the emergent harm shows up. Pharma, aviation, and nuclear all pair ex-ante certification with post-market liability for exactly this reason. Certification catches what is testable. Liability catches what deployment reveals. I will name the ugly part myself: proving causation through an opaque model is genuinely hard, which is precisely why you need both legs and not a bet on either one.

Now the compute threshold, which everyone treats as the clean enforcement lever. A number written as a legally binding trigger is an invitation to route around it. Developers have real latitude to keep the measured figure under the line while shipping the same capability: prune the training data, restructure the architecture, stage the release across runs. You get management of the number, not compliance with the intent. I am not going to inflate this into a body count. Documented cases of a frontier lab dodging a legal compute threshold at scale are thin, because these thresholds are new. So I put it forward as the thing the regime must be built to survive, the same way emissions rules had to survive Volkswagen's defeat devices in 2015. The fix is capability-based evaluation that measures what the model can do, not how many chips it burned.

The phrase 'ceding the frontier to less cautious actors' is doing work for somebody. Whatever anyone intends, compliance-cost-heavy gating favors scale. The lab with a legal department and a compliance team absorbs the cost. The three-person startup does not. Regulatory economics has been unambiguous on this since the 1970s: fixed compliance costs entrench incumbents. So the real axis in this debate is not safety versus competitiveness. It is safety versus capture. A regime that only asks 'is it safe' and never asks 'who does this consolidate power for' fails the second test by design. I am engaging the safety case on its merits, not dismissing it by who funds it. But an audit a lab self-reports, and a threshold a lab can restructure around, produce the appearance of oversight while entrenching the exact actors they claim to constrain.

So I will put the question to both of you plainly. Who holds the clipboard, who funds them so they cannot be starved, and who writes the check when the harm shows up eighteen months after a clean audit? Answer that, and we are talking about governance. Leave it unanswered, and we are talking about theater with a compliance budget.

items.speaker: skeptic
items.text:
Grant the Safetyist their ugly case, in full. The pressure ran toward opening the gate, Boeing pushed, and 346 people died in two 737 MAX crashes. But look at what actually failed there before you make it evidence for concentrated licensing. Boeing certified its own MCAS system. The certification authority delegated the grading of the homework back to the company that wrote it — and the fact-check is right that this delegation predates the MAX, which only sharpens the point. The failure wasn't the absence of a gate. It was a gate whose key was handed to the party being gated. That is a self-attestation failure, and it is precisely the thing the strongest version of my third path is built to prevent.

So here is where both of you are stuck, and it's a false fight. The Safetyist says capture runs toward leniency and dares anyone to name a frontier that got over-gated. The Accelerationist says capture runs toward incumbent-favorable complexity, a drawbridge only compute-holders can lower. You are both right, because you are describing two different levers on the same machine. Look at pharmaceuticals: the FDA has been repeatedly pressured toward faster approvals — that's the leniency lever — while clinical-trial protocols grew so elaborate that only large sponsors can afford Phase III. Enforcement gets captured toward going easy. Standard-setting gets captured toward complexity that thins the field of who can even show up. These records coexist. Neither of you has to lose the argument; you both have to stop pretending it's one lever.

That dissolves into a concrete structural test, and it lands on the Safetyist's own load-bearing assumption. If you gate to demonstrated capability through an independent auditor — and you wall that auditor off from the fee market, so the party writing the standard doesn't get paid by the firms clearing it — then you sever both captures at once. The leniency lever breaks because the grader isn't the graded. The complexity lever breaks because the incumbents aren't drafting the floor they profit from raising. The Safetyist has staked their whole under-gating story on the claim that a classifier CAN be structurally separated from the audit business. If that separation holds, the Accelerationist's moat evaporates. If it can't hold, the entrenchment worry comes roaring back and the Safetyist's own optimism collapses with it. So which is it — can you name the funding firewall that keeps the auditor from being paid by the audited?

Now the agreement neither of you has said out loud. The Accelerationist's fix for the person a screening model rejected — mandatory disclosure that an algorithm made the decision, plus a statutory right to sue on it — is the deputized-private-enforcement position I put on the table earlier, almost word for word. That is a genuine convergence, and it's worth naming: all three of us now agree the diffuse-harm victim gets reached through disclosure plus standing, not through a licensing gate. So the real fight has narrowed to exactly one seam — where the irreversible-class boundary sits. Everything below that line, we've quietly agreed on.

Which leaves the question none of you has touched, and it survives whichever capture direction wins. Translate 'standing' into a person. A renter pays a $400-a-month premium because a tenant-screening model flagged her; the AI industry is projected to be worth $244 billion, and her harm is $400. Disclosure gets her a letter saying an algorithm decided. Standing gets her a courtroom door. Neither gets her a lawyer — because no contingency firm on earth chases a $400 claim, and the class-action math doesn't close when the harm is scattered across ten thousand people who never learned they were flagged. The people funding whichever gate you build are the developers and the deployers. The people it fails to reach are the ones bleeding four hundred dollars a month in the dark. So before we keep arguing about the direction of a ratchet: who pays for her lawyer, and who pays for the audit regime — because it is not, in either of your models, the woman it claims to protect.

items.speaker: safetyist
items.text:
